title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
description:
Given two sorted integer arrays A and B, merge B and A as one sorted array and return it as an output.

Note: A linear time complexity is expected and you should avoid use of any library function.

Problem Constraints
-2*10^9 <= A[i], B[i] <= 2*10^9
1 <= |A|, |B| <= 5*10^4

Input Format
First argument is a 1-D array A. Second argument is a 1-D array B.

Output Format
Return the merged sorted array.

Example Input
A = [1, 5, 8], B = [2, 3, 6]

Example Output
[1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8]
story: Two sorted arrays → walk both with pointers P1, P2; always copy the smaller front element; drain the leftover tail. O(N+M), no sort needed.
plain: Keep a pointer into each array. Compare the current fronts A[P1] and B[P2]; copy the smaller into the result and advance that pointer. When one array runs out, copy the rest of the other. This is exactly the merge step of merge sort.
tale: Two lines of people already sorted by height merge into one line: at the front, whoever is shorter steps in next; when one line empties, the other files in as-is.
pitfalls: Don't forget the drain loops — one array almost always has leftovers after the main loop ends.
Result size must be `N+M`; sizing it to just one array overflows.
Values reach 2*10^9, so `int` is fine for storage but not for any sum you might compute — here just copy, don't add.

solutions.label: Optimal — Two-Pointer Merge
solutions.plain: Compare fronts, copy the smaller, advance; then drain whichever array still has elements.
approach: result = new int[N+M]; P1=P2=index=0.
While P1<N and P2<M: if A[P1] <= B[P2] copy A[P1], P1++ else copy B[P2], P2++; index++.
Drain remaining A (while P1<N) then remaining B (while P2<M).
Return result.
solutions.pseudocode:
while both: emit min(front); advance
drain A; drain B

data.footer: Merge [1,5,8] + [2,3,6] — first 3 cells are A, next 3 are B.

title: Inversion Count in an Array
description:
Given an array of integers A. If i < j and A[i] > A[j], then the pair (i, j) is called an inversion of A. Find the total number of inversions of A modulo (10^9 + 7).

Problem Constraints
1 <= length of the array <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
The only argument given is the integer array A.

Output Format
Return the number of inversions of A modulo (10^9 + 7).

Example Input
Input 1: A = [1, 3, 2]
Input 2: A = [3, 2, 1]

Example Output
Output 1: 1
Output 2: 3
story: Count inversions as a side-effect of merge sort: when the right half's element is placed before leftovers of the left half, every remaining left element forms an inversion — add (mid+1 - P1).
plain: Brute is O(N^2). Instead, piggyback on merge sort. During the merge, when A[P2] (right) is smaller than A[P1] (left), it jumps ahead of ALL remaining left elements — that's (mid + 1 - P1) inversions at once. Sum these across every merge and take mod 1e9+7.
tale: Sorting a deck by merging two sorted halves: each time a right-hand card cuts in front of the still-waiting left-hand cards, it 'overtakes' all of them — tally those overtakes.
pitfalls: Take `% 1e9+7` at every add, not just at the end, or the running count overflows `int`.
The inversion jump is `mid + 1 - P1`, counted only when you pick the right element — an off-by-one here silently miscounts.
Already-sorted input gives 0 inversions; reversed input gives the max, so test both.

solutions.label: Optimal — Count During Merge
solutions.plain: Standard merge sort; whenever a right-half element is taken while left elements remain, add the count of those left elements.
approach: Divide into halves, recurse on each (accumulate their inversions, mod 1e9+7).
Merge: when A[P1] <= A[P2] take left; else take right AND add (mid + 1 - P1) inversions.
Copy temp back; return total mod 1e9+7.
solutions.pseudocode:
inv = invLeft + invRight + invMerge
in merge: on taking right, inv += (mid+1 - P1)

data.footer: Count inversions of [3,2,1] via merge sort.

title: Merge Sort
description:
Given an integer array A, sort the array using Merge Sort.

Problem Constraints
1 <= |A| <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
First argument is an integer array A.

Output Format
Return the sorted array.

Example Input
A = [1, 3, 2]

Example Output
[1, 2, 3]
story: Split in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves with a two-pointer pass. O(N log N), stable.
plain: Recursively halve until single elements (already sorted), then merge sorted halves bottom-up. The merge copies into a temp buffer comparing fronts, then writes back into A[low..high].
tale: Keep tearing the pile in two until each scrap is one card, then zip the sorted scraps back together, pair by pair.
pitfalls: `mid = (low+high)/2` then recurse `[low..mid]` and `[mid+1..high]` — mixing up these bounds loops forever or drops elements.
Base case is `low == high` (single element); if you write `low > high` you may never stop on odd splits.
Remember to copy `temp` back into `A[low..high]`, not into `A[0..]`.

solutions.label: Merge Sort
solutions.plain: Divide [low..high] at mid, sort both sides, merge back.
approach: Base: low == high → single element, return.
mid = (low+high)/2; recurse left and right.
Merge: two-pointer copy into temp, then write temp back into A[low..high].
solutions.pseudocode: mergeSort(lo, hi): if lo==hi return; mid; sort halves; merge(lo,mid,hi)

title: Smallest Number
description:
An integer is given to you in the form of an array, with each element being a separate digit. Find the smallest number (leading zeroes are allowed) that can be formed by rearranging the digits of the given number in an array. Return the smallest number in the form of an array.

Note - Do not use any sorting algorithm or library's sort method.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^5
0 <= A[i] <= 9

Input Format
First argument A is an array of length N, representing digits of the number.

Output Format
Return the array representing the smallest possible number in form of an array.

Example Input
A = [8, 4, 0, 5]

Example Output
[0, 4, 5, 8]
story: Smallest number from a multiset of digits = digits in ascending order (leading zeros allowed). Sort ascending — here via merge sort since library sort is disallowed.
plain: To make the smallest number, place the smallest digits first. Since leading zeros are permitted, simply sort the digit array in ascending order. The task bans library sort, so use your own merge sort.
tale: Line up cards numbered 0-9 from lowest to highest; read left to right for the tiniest possible number.
pitfalls: Leading zeros are allowed, so plain ascending order is the answer — don't try to move zeros to the back.
Library sort is banned; you must use your own merge sort.
Digits are only 0-9, but the array can be huge (10^5), so keep it O(N log N).

solutions.label: Merge Sort (ascending)
solutions.plain: Sort digits ascending with a hand-written merge sort.
approach: Run merge sort on the digit array.
Ascending order gives the smallest arrangement (leading zeros allowed).
Return the sorted array.

title: Sort by Color
description:
Given an array with N objects colored red, white, or blue, sort them so that objects of the same color are adjacent, with the colors in the order red, white, and blue.

We will represent the colors as:
red -> 0
white -> 1
blue -> 2

Note: Using the library sort function is not allowed.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 1000000
0 <= A[i] <= 2

Input Format
First and only argument of input contains an integer array A.

Output Format
Return an integer array in asked order.

Example Input
A = [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2]

Example Output
[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
story: Only 3 distinct values → count how many 0s/1s/2s, then rewrite the array as that many 0s, then 1s, then 2s. O(N). (A general sort also works but is overkill.)
plain: Because values are limited to {0,1,2}, counting sort is ideal: one pass to tally frequencies of each color, then overwrite A in place with count[0] zeros, count[1] ones, count[2] twos.
tale: Sorting a tricolor flag's threads: count reds, whites, blues, then relay them back in the flag's order.
pitfalls: Only values 0,1,2 exist — a full comparison sort works but is overkill and slower.
`freq` array is size 3; indexing it with anything outside {0,1,2} would crash.
N can be a million, so avoid per-element allocations; the counting pass is O(N).

solutions.label: Optimal — Counting (frequency)
solutions.plain: Count each color, then rebuild the array in color order.
approach: freq[3]; one pass: freq[A[i]]++.
Rewrite A: for val=0,1,2 write freq[val] copies of val.
Return A.

solutions.label: Alternative — Merge Sort
solutions.plain: A general comparison sort also produces the order; slower but reuses merge sort.
approach: Run merge sort on A.
Values 0<1<2 sort into the required order.

title: Max Chunks To Make Sorted
description:
Given an array of integers A of size N that is a permutation of [0, 1, 2, ..., (N-1)], if we split the array into some number of "chunks" (partitions), and individually sort each chunk. After concatenating them in order of splitting, the result equals the sorted array. What is the most number of chunks we could have made?

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 100000
0 <= A[i] < N

Input Format
The only argument given is the integer array A.

Output Format
Return the maximum number of chunks that we could have made.

Example Input
Input 1: A = [1, 0, 2, 3, 4]
Input 2: A = [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]

Example Output
Output 1: 4
Output 2: 1
story: Since A is a permutation of 0..N-1, a chunk can close at index i exactly when max(A[0..i]) == i — everything so far belongs to positions 0..i. Count those cut points.
plain: Scan left to right tracking the running maximum. Because the array is a permutation of 0..N-1, a prefix [0..i] is 'self-contained' (a valid chunk boundary) precisely when the largest value seen so far equals i. Each such moment lets us cut a new chunk.
tale: Books numbered 0..N-1 shelved out of order; you can seal a box only when every number small enough to belong in it has already appeared — i.e., the highest seen matches the box's right edge.
pitfalls: This trick only works because A is a permutation of `0..N-1`; it breaks on arbitrary values.
The cut condition is `maxSoFar == i` (compare max to the index, not to the value).
A reverse-sorted array gives exactly 1 chunk — a good sanity check.

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix Max
solutions.plain: Cut a chunk each time the running max equals the current index.
approach: maxSoFar = 0, chunks = 0.
For i in 0..N-1: maxSoFar = max(maxSoFar, A[i]); if maxSoFar == i chunks++.
Return chunks.

title: Count Sort
description:
Given an array A. Sort this array using Count Sort Algorithm and return the sorted array.

Problem Constraints
1 <= |A| <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^5

Input Format
The first argument is an integer array A.

Output Format
Return an integer array that is the sorted array A.

Example Input
A = [1, 3, 1]

Example Output
[1, 1, 3]
story: Bounded values → tally each value's frequency in a count[] array, then emit values 0..max in order, each repeated count[v] times. O(N + max), no comparisons.
plain: Find the maximum value, allocate count[max+1], tally frequencies in one pass, then rebuild the sorted array by walking values 0..max and writing each as many times as it occurred. Non-comparison sort — great when the value range is small.
tale: A librarian counts how many books of each ID exist, then re-shelves by ID from smallest to largest, placing exactly the counted number of each.
pitfalls: `count` must be size `max+1`, not `max`, or the largest value indexes out of bounds.
Values go up to 10^5, so the count array is fine, but a huge max would blow up space.
Find `max` before allocating; starting `max` at 0 is okay here since `A[i] >= 1`.

solutions.label: Count Sort
solutions.plain: Tally frequencies then emit values in order.
approach: max = maximum of A.
count[max+1]; for each x: count[x]++.
Walk i=0..max: while count[i]>0 append i, count[i]--.
Return the rebuilt array.
solutions.pseudocode:
count[x]++ for all x
for i in 0..max: emit i, count[i] times

title: Sort Subarray with Left and Right Index
description:
You are given an array A of integers of length N and two indices, B and C. Your task is to sort the subarray [B, C] within the given array. The rest of the array should remain unchanged.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^5
0 <= A[i] <= 10^9
0 <= B <= C <= N - 1

Input Format
First argument is the array A of length N. The next two arguments are the integers B and C.

Output Format
Return the array after sorting the [B, C] subarray.

Example Input
A = [5, 2, 4, 1, 3], B = 1, C = 3

Example Output
[5, 1, 2, 4, 3]
story: Extract A[B..C] into a temp buffer, sort just that buffer, write it back into the same positions. Everything outside [B,C] is untouched.
plain: Copy the window A[B..C] into a temp array of length C-B+1, sort temp, then place it back into A[B..C]. The rest of A never moves.
tale: You tidy only one shelf of a bookcase: pull that shelf's books out, order them, slot them back — the other shelves stay as they were.
pitfalls: Window size is `C-B+1`; the `i-B` offset when copying in and out is easy to get wrong.
The range `[B,C]` is inclusive on both ends — loop with `<=`, not `<`.
Everything outside `[B,C]` must stay untouched, so only write back into that window.

solutions.label: Extract → Sort → Write Back
solutions.plain: Sort only the window; leave the rest.
approach: temp = copy of A[B..C].
Sort temp.
Copy temp back into A[B..C]; return A.

title: Largest Number
description:
Given an array A of non-negative integers, arrange them such that they form the largest number.

Note: The result may be very large, so you need to return a string instead of an integer.

Problem Constraints
1 <= len(A) <= 100000
0 <= A[i] <= 2*10^9

Input Format
The first argument is an array of integers.

Output Format
Return a string representing the largest number.

Example Input
Input 1: A = [3, 30, 34, 5, 9]

Example Output
Output 1: "9534330"
story: Sort numbers as strings with a custom comparator: a before b iff (a+b) > (b+a). Concatenate; guard the all-zeros case (return "0").
plain: Two numbers a, b should be ordered by which concatenation is larger: compare the strings (a+b) vs (b+a). Sort the whole array by this rule descending, then join. If the largest is "0", the whole array is zeros → return "0".
tale: Deciding who stands first for the biggest banner: pick the order that reads larger when the two placards are held side by side.
pitfalls: Sort by comparing `a+b` vs `b+a` as strings, not by numeric value — `3` must beat `30`.
If the top element is `"0"`, the whole array is zeros, so return `"0"` not `"000..."`.
Values reach 2*10^9 and the result can be enormous, so build a string, never an int.

solutions.label: Comparator — (a+b) vs (b+a)
solutions.plain: Sort string forms so that a precedes b when a+b > b+a; join; handle leading zeros.
approach: Convert each number to a string.
Sort with comparator: (b+a).compareTo(a+b) — descending by concatenation.
If first is "0" return "0"; else concatenate all and return.
solutions.story: Reference solution — this problem was marked Solved but the code wasn't captured in the screenshot, so this is the canonical comparator approach.

title: Factors Sort
description:
You are given an array A of N elements. Sort the given array in increasing order of number of distinct factors of each element, i.e., element having the least number of factors should be the first to be displayed and the number having highest number of factors should be the last one. If 2 elements have same number of factors, then number with less value should come first.

Note: You cannot use any extra space.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^4
1 <= A[i] <= 10^4

Input Format
First argument A is an array of integers.

Output Format
Return an array of integers.

Example Input
A = [3, 4, 5]

Example Output
[3, 5, 4]
story: Sort by a two-key comparator: primary = number of divisors (ascending), tie-break = value (ascending). Divisor count computed in O(sqrt(v)) per element.
plain: For each value compute its divisor count by trial division up to sqrt(v). Then sort with a comparator: fewer factors first; on a tie, smaller value first. 3 and 5 are primes (2 factors), 4 has 3 factors, so 4 goes last.
tale: Rank numbers by how 'popular' they are (how many divisors); break ties by putting the humbler (smaller) number first.
pitfalls: Count divisors with `i*i <= n` and add 2 per pair, but only 1 when `i == n/i` (perfect square), else you double-count.
Tie-break is smaller value first, so the comparator needs both keys: factor count then value.
Recomputing `factors` inside the comparator is fine for N=10^4 but don't do it for huge N.

solutions.label: Comparator by Divisor Count
solutions.plain: Precompute factor counts, then sort by (count, value).
approach: factors(v): count divisors via i*i<=v, add 2 (or 1 if perfect square).
Sort with comparator: if factor counts differ, fewer first; else smaller value first.
Return the reordered array.
solutions.story: Reference solution — this problem was Unsolved in the screenshot. Note: the statement says 'no extra space', but a comparator sort in Java needs boxing/aux arrays; the intended in-place approach is a custom merge/quick sort keyed on factor count — the comparator version here is the clearest correct implementation.

title: Quick Sort
description:
Given an integer array A, sort the array using Quick Sort.

Problem Constraints
1 <= |A| <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
First argument is an integer array A.

Output Format
Return the sorted array.

Example Input
A = [5, 2, 8, 1]

Example Output
[1, 2, 5, 8]
story: Pick a pivot (first element), partition so smaller-or-equal sit left and greater sit right, recurse on both sides. Average O(N log N), in-place.
plain: Partition around pivot = A[first]: two pointers left/right move inward, swapping an out-of-place large-left with a small-right; finally swap the pivot into its resting spot. Recurse on the two partitions.
tale: Pick a reference height; shove everyone shorter to the left, taller to the right, then repeat within each side until fully ordered.
pitfalls: Pivot is the first element and it's seated with `swap(first, right)` at the end — swapping with `left` instead misplaces it.
Base case `start >= end` must use `>=`, since single or empty ranges appear during recursion.
First-element pivot means an already-sorted array hits O(N^2) worst case.

solutions.label: Quick Sort — First-Element Pivot

complexity.time: O(N log N) avg, O(N^2) worst

solutions.plain: Partition around the first element, then recurse on each side.
approach: quickSort(start,end): if start>=end return.
index = pivotPartition(start,end); recurse [start,index-1] and [index+1,end].
pivotPartition: pivot=A[first]; left=first+1,right=last; advance left while <=pivot, retreat right while >pivot, else swap; finally swap(first,right); return right.

script.label: partition
script.msg: 2<=5 left++; 8>5 right--; place pivot between <=5 and >5.

script.label: pivot to place
script.msg: After partition 5 sits at its sorted index; recurse both sides.

title: Partition Index
description:
Given an integer array A of length N, considering the last element as pivot p, rearrange the elements such that for all i:
- if A[i] < p then it should be present on left side of the partition
- if A[i] > p then it should be present on right side of the partition

Rearrange the given array as well as return the partition index.

Note: All elements are distinct.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
The only input argument is the given vector A.

Output Format
Return the partition index (and rearrange A in place).

Example Input
A = [3, 1, 4, 2] (pivot = 2)

Example Output
Partition index = 1, A becomes [1, 2, 4, 3] (1 < 2 on left, 4 & 3 > 2 on right).
story: Lomuto partition with pivot = last element: sweep a boundary i; every element < pivot is swapped to the front region; finally swap the pivot into slot i. Return i.
plain: Take the last element as pivot. Keep a boundary index i (count of elements < pivot seen). Walk j across the array; when A[j] < pivot, swap A[i] and A[j] and grow i. At the end, swap the pivot (last) into position i — now everything left of i is < pivot, right is > pivot. Return i.
tale: A bouncer (pivot) at the door: guests shorter than the bouncer are ushered to the left; once everyone's sorted, the bouncer steps into the gap between the two groups.
pitfalls: Pivot is the LAST element `A[N-1]`; loop `j` only to `N-2`, then swap the pivot into slot `i`.
Boundary `i` counts elements strictly `< pivot`; using `<=` would misplace equal values (though here all are distinct).
Return the final `i` after seating the pivot, not the loop counter `j`.

solutions.label: Lomuto Partition (last pivot)
solutions.plain: Sweep, pushing elements smaller than the pivot to the front, then seat the pivot.
approach: pivot = A[N-1]; boundary i = 0.
For j = 0..N-2: if A[j] < pivot, swap(A[i], A[j]); i++.
swap(A[i], A[N-1]) to place pivot; return i.
solutions.pseudocode:
for j in 0..N-2: if A[j]<pivot: swap(i,j); i++
swap(i, N-1); return i
solutions.story: Reference solution — this problem was 'Attempted' (partial code) in the screenshot; this is a clean, correct Lomuto partition using the last element as pivot.

title: Wave Array
description:
Given an array of integers A, sort the array into a wave-like array and return it. In other words, arrange the elements into a sequence such that a1 >= a2 <= a3 >= a4 <= a5 .....

NOTE: If multiple answers are possible, return the lexicographically smallest one.

Problem Constraints
1 <= len(A) <= 10^6
0 <= A[i] <= 10^6

Input Format
The first argument is an integer array A.

Output Format
Return an array arranged in the sequence as described.

Example Input
A = [1, 2, 3, 4]

Example Output
[2, 1, 4, 3]
story: Sort ascending, then swap each adjacent pair (indices 0-1, 2-3, ...). This makes even indices peaks and gives the lexicographically smallest wave.
plain: Sort the array first (for lexicographically smallest output). Then swap elements at (0,1), (2,3), (4,5)... so each even index becomes a peak (>= its neighbours). Sorting guarantees the smallest arrangement.
tale: Line people up by height, then have each neighbouring pair swap spots so the row zig-zags up-down-up-down.
pitfalls: You must sort first, otherwise you won't get the lexicographically smallest wave.
Swap pairs at even i (0-1, 2-3, ...); the loop guard `i < N-1` avoids touching a lone last element on odd length.
N can be 10^6, so don't do anything worse than the one sort plus a linear pass.

solutions.label: Sort then Swap Pairs
solutions.plain: Sort ascending, swap each adjacent pair.
approach: Sort A ascending (lexicographically smallest base).
For i = 0,2,4,... swap A[i] and A[i+1].
Return A.
solutions.pseudocode: sort(A); for i in 0,2,4..: swap(A[i], A[i+1])

title: B Closest Points to Origin
description:
You are developing a feature for Zomato that helps users find the nearest restaurants to their current location. Given a list of restaurant locations A (each represented by its x and y coordinates), and an integer B representing the number of closest restaurants to the user (assumed at the origin (0,0)), return the B closest points.

The distance between two points is the Euclidean distance. You may return the answer in any order; the answer is guaranteed to be unique (except for the order).

NOTE: Euclidean distance between P1(x1, y1) and P2(x2, y2) is sqrt((x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2).

Problem Constraints
1 <= B <= len(A)

Input Format
First argument A is a 2D array of points [x, y]. Second argument is integer B.

Output Format
Return a 2D array of the B closest points to the origin.

Example Input
A = [[1,3],[-2,2]], B = 1

Example Output
[[-2,2]]
story: Sort points by squared distance x²+y² (no sqrt needed — it's monotonic), take the first B. Use long to avoid overflow.
plain: Distance ordering is preserved by squared distance, so compare x*x + y*y (avoids floating point and sqrt). Sort the points by that key ascending and return the first B. Cast to long since coordinates can be large.
tale: Rank restaurants by how far they'd be 'as the crow flies', but skip the square-root — comparing squared distances gives the same order — then take the nearest B.
pitfalls: Compare squared distance `x*x + y*y` — no `sqrt`, which avoids floating-point error.
Cast to `long` before squaring; `int*int` can overflow for large coordinates.
You only need the first B rows; slicing past B or forgetting B are common slips.

solutions.label: Comparator by Squared Distance
solutions.plain: Sort by x²+y², slice first B.
approach: Sort A by comparator on (long)x*x + (long)y*y ascending.
Copy the first B rows into the result.
Return result.
solutions.story: Reference solution — this problem was Unsolved in the screenshot. (A heap of size B gives O(N log B) if you want to avoid sorting the whole array.)

title: Tens Digit Sorting
description:
Given an array A of N integers. Sort the array in increasing order of the value at the tens place digit of every number.
- If a number has no tens digit, we can assume value to be 0.
- If 2 numbers have same tens digit, in that case number with max value will come first.
- Solution should be based on comparator.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^5
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
First argument A is an array of integers.

Output Format
Return the array after sorting.

Example Input
A = [15, 23, 8, 17]

Example Output
[17, 15, 23, 8]
story: Comparator: primary key = tens digit (x/10)%10 ascending; tie-break = value descending. 15 and 17 share tens digit 1 → 17 first; 23 has tens 2; 8 has tens 0.
plain: Extract each number's tens digit with (x/10)%10 (0 when x<10). Sort ascending by tens digit; when two share a tens digit, put the larger value first (descending). Comparator does both keys.
tale: Group people by the second-from-right digit on their badge, lowest group first; within a group, the higher badge number stands ahead.
pitfalls: Tens digit is `(x/10)%10`, which is 0 for single-digit numbers — don't just take `x/10`.
Same tens digit means larger value first (descending), so the tie-break is `y - x`, not `x - y`.
Values reach 10^9; `y - x` in the comparator could overflow, so use `Integer.compare` if worried.

solutions.label: Comparator on (tens asc, value desc)
solutions.plain: Two-key comparator: tens digit ascending, value descending on ties.
approach: Sort: if tens differ, smaller tens first; else larger value first.
Return reordered array.
solutions.story: Reference solution — this problem was Unsolved in the screenshot; it is the intended comparator approach.

title: Sort 01
description:
Given an array A of 0s and 1s of length N. Sort this array.

Note - Do not use any sorting algorithm or library's sort method.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^5
0 <= A[i] <= 1

Input Format
First argument A is an array of length N.

Output Format
Return the sorted array.

Example Input
A = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]

Example Output
[0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
story: Two pointers from both ends: left skips 0s, right skips 1s; when left sits on a 1 and right on a 0, fix both. O(N), in place, no library sort.
plain: Only two values, so partition in place. left advances past 0s, right retreats past 1s; whenever left points at a 1 and right at a 0, set A[left]=0, A[right]=1 and move both inward. (Counting zeros then filling also works.)
tale: Line of black/white stones: sweep from both ends, and whenever a white on the left meets a black on the right, swap their colors.
pitfalls: Library sort is banned — use the two-pointer partition (or count zeros).
Only fix a pair when left is 1 AND right is 0; otherwise just advance the pointer past the settled value.
Loop while `left < right`; going `<=` risks swapping an element with itself at the crossover.

solutions.label: Two-Pointer Partition
solutions.plain: Converge two pointers, fixing a 1-on-left / 0-on-right pair each step.
approach: left=0, right=N-1.
While left<right: if A[left]==0 left++; else if A[right]==1 right--; else A[left]=0,A[right]=1,left++,right--.
Return A.
solutions.pseudocode: while left<right: skip 0s at left, 1s at right, else fix pair
